title: 3-Read Friday #8: Problem Solving, Self-Explanation Prompts, and Mathematical Storytelling
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Issue eight centers on how students learn to reason through mathematics rather than simply practice it. Barton returns to Craig Latimir for a third time in the newsletter's short run, covering his post on problem-solving, which opens with the counter-intuitive point that students don't get better at problem-solving simply by solving more problems, and highlights Latimir's "number-free problems" and "zoom-in zoom-out" strategies. He then covers the third instalment of Alex Blanksby's Five Ways series, on self-explanation prompts, referencing Renkl's 1998 finding that most students don't spontaneously self-explain without support. He closes with Dan Meyer's revisiting of his own older "Three Acts of a Mathematical Story" post, which Barton says he was "obsessed" with, tying it to Willingham's work on the power of story for engagement and retention. All three items concern how students construct mathematical understanding, keeping the issue in Learning & Curriculum.
points: Barton highlights Latimir's counter-intuitive claim that repeated problem-solving practice alone does not build problem-solving skill, and singles out "number-free problems" as the more useful strategy.
He connects Blanksby's self-explanation prompts directly to Renkl's 1998 research finding that most students need explicit support to self-explain at all.
He frames Meyer's Three-Act Math structure as personally formative, describing his own past "obsession" with it and its grounding in Willingham's research on story and retention.
quotes: He begins with a realisation that hit me hard a few years ago: students don’t get better at problem-solving by simply solving more problems.
But the strength of this post is in the two practical strategies Craig offers to help students become better problem solvers: Number-free problems and Zoom-in Zoom-out.

There are swatches of research that extol the power of self-explaining, but then there is Renkl’s 1998 paper that suggests the majority of students do not spontaneously self-explain and so need our support to do so.
I was obsessed - and I mean, obsessed - with Dan’s 3-Act Math structure.
It taps into Dan Willingham’s work on the power of stories to engage and support retention, and turns it into a format teachers can use in lessons: the conflict, the tools, the resolution.
